evidence.text: The entry analyzes 上 as an indicative graph: a short mark above a longer reference line indicates the upper side. It describes some oracle-bone examples with a curved baseline, later often straightened because carving a horizontal line was easier. It reports that early oracle-bone and bronze forms could resemble 二, with a vertical stroke added in many late Spring-and-Autumn forms to distinguish the graph. Its examples include Shang-inscription 上帝 and 上甲, Zhou-bronze spatial uses, and a Chu-script form with 辵 added as a semantic element for upward movement. These are the dictionary's reports, not independent inspection of each inscription.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: 香港教育局 字源考釋
evidence.field: 字形流變 / 字形解說
evidence.text: The character-specific account presents oracle-bone 上 as two horizontal strokes: a longer lower stroke as a reference line and a shorter upper stroke marking above. It says later bronze and small-seal forms altered the upper stroke to a vertical one to avoid confusion with 二, and the modern standard form adds a dot. This differs in its description of the earliest line from CUHK's curved-baseline account; both describe a positional marker above a reference line.
evidence.title: 字源考釋 - 上

evidence.source: 中央研究院 漢字構形資料庫
evidence.text: The entry describes the oracle-bone form as two horizontal strokes, the lower longer line representing the horizon and the upper shorter stroke indicating above. It says a later vertical stroke helped distinguish 上 from 二. It is a paleographic account, not a primary artifact image.
evidence.title: 漢字「上」：字形演變

evidence.source: 許慎《說文解字》 text as presented by Taiwan Ministry of Education variant dictionary
evidence.text: The dictionary reports that the received Da Xu edition of Shuowen has 丄, glossed ‘high’ and classed as 指事, then calls 上 the seal-script form; Duan Yucai's edition instead prints 二 as the head form. This documents a textual/editorial difference in the received Shuowen tradition and Han lexicographic analysis, not independent evidence for Shang graphic history.
evidence.title: 教育部《異體字字典》 — 上

evidence.field: 上 / semantic uses by inscriptional period
evidence.text: The entry reports 上帝, 上甲, and contrasting 上/下 contexts in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions; it reports spatial ‘above’ and ‘at/on the side of’ in Zhou bronze inscriptions and 上 in the sense ‘more than’ in a Spring-and-Autumn tally. It reports a later traditional-literature extension to ruler, elder, or one in authority, citing Guangya and Liji. These reports support early spatial and lexical uses, but do not give a secure dated sequence for every later sense or independently establish the semantic links.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫 — 漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.field: 國風・陳・宛丘 / poem text
evidence.text: The transmitted poem contains ‘宛丘之上兮’ and, in the next line, ‘宛丘之下’; this is an attested locative contrast ‘on/at the upper part of Want Hill.’ The page supplies the text but does not date this specific written witness; it should not be treated as a securely dated physical inscription.
evidence.title: 詩經/宛丘

evidence.field: File description, object description, inscription text, provenance and licensing
evidence.text: The page identifies the object as an incised Shang-dynasty ox scapula attributed to the Li diviner group, period II, and dates it to the early 12th century BC. Its transcription includes 上甲 in a sacrificial context. This is a real artifact photograph candidate, but the page does not isolate or label the exact 上 glyph within the image. It is released under CC BY-SA/GFDL terms on the description page.
evidence.title: File:Orakelknochen.JPG

Its description establishes the object class and provenance, but it does not identify a 上 inscription in the object, so it is not a character-specific glyph candidate.

gaps: The earliest graphic accounts agree that 上 is an indicative positional marker above a reference line, but disagree over whether the early reference line was curved or horizontal. No primary artifact image was visually inspected here to adjudicate this variation.

The selected Shang bone photograph depicts an inscribed artifact and its transcription includes 上甲, but the character is not individually highlighted or identified in the image description; a separate visual review is needed before treating it as an educational close-up of 上.

The CUHK period-specific examples and uses are reported by a secondary paleographic dictionary. Except for the Commons inscription transcription of 上甲, the named artifacts were not independently opened and checked in this pass.
The exact derivation of senses such as ‘superior’, ‘ruler’, and verbal ‘ascend/send up’ is not established chronologically. A dictionary gloss sequence is not evidence for that progression.

The supplied local Baxter–Sagart readings are three separate lexical rows: 上 MC dzyangX / OC *Cə-daŋʔ (‘ascend’), MC dzyangX / OC *m-daŋʔ (‘to put up’), and MC dzyangH / OC *daŋʔ-s (‘top, above’). No inspected external primary table was found in this pass, so these are local dataset rows rather than externally verified evidence.
The individual Unicode Unihan page was inaccessible. Local kMandarin 上 = shàng is supplied but not independently verified against the upstream record.
The Xiaoxuetang form query returned 401 and no candidates; no Xiaoxuetang image was selected. The unrelated British Library bone image was not selected because its description does not tie it to 上.
No component or phonetic element is proposed: the inspected character-specific accounts analyze 上 as an indicative graph.

items.caption: A Shang oracle-bone inscription whose published transcription includes 上甲. The source associates the bone with the early 12th century BC; the individual 上 glyph is not marked separately in the file description.
